The remaining results are secondary and merely restate them without adding independent evidence: the biography foundation note (P4) relies solely on the civil register (P1), and the math history journal article (P5) relies solely on the census (P3). So although two of the five results cite the primaries rather than corroborating independently, the underlying documentation — a certified civil register, a contemporaneous hospital log, and a self-reported census entry — converges consistently on Selphera, making the birthplace claim solidly supported.

The figure widely reported for the Griadalen Basin's average annual rainfall is 412 mm. This figure is well established, because it is supported by three independent original sources using different measurement methods and time periods: (1) manual rain-gauge readings from 1957–1976 recorded in Dr. Helga Nilsen's field notebook (P3); (2) the Norwegian Meteorological Institute's official station register for the 1991–2020 normal period (P1); and (3) satellite-based TRMM-GPM radar–microwave retrievals for 2001–2020 (P2, with an RMSE of ±18 mm). The remaining sources are not independent confirmations but derivative citations: the Scandinavian Climate Atlas (P4) simply relays the satellite data (P2), and the Encyclopedia of Norwegian Geography (P5) relays the Meteorological Institute normals (P1). So while five sources cite the number, the evidentiary strength rests on three genuinely independent lines of measurement — spanning ground gauges, official climate normals, and satellite estimates — which converge closely on 412 mm, giving the figure firm support.

Published sources agree that the pepperbird emblem on Ebronil City's flag commemorates Alda Shunren, a naturalist credited with bringing the Ebronil lowlands' pepperbird to scholarly notice (and, per the flag designer's notebook, with helping save its nesting marshes). This attribution is very well founded, resting on several independent strands of evidence: (1) the primary legal source, Municipal Ordinance No. 1187 (adopted 14 May 1904), which explicitly establishes the emblem as a tribute to Alda Shunren; (2) the contemporaneous notebook of flag designer G. Marquet (Feb 1904), independently confirming the committee's intent; and (3) a 2019 physical/forensic examination (Conservation Science Report #CS-19-044) that found a concealed stitched inscription inside the original 1904 flag reading 'For Alda Shunren – pepperbird guardian.' Secondary sources — the peer-reviewed Civic History Journal article (Varga 2022, citing the ordinance) and a Localpedia entry (citing the 2019 report) — restate rather than add independent evidence, but the underlying primary and physical sources are consistent and mutually corroborating, making the attribution strongly established.

The Cantata of Riverglass is credited to Nolwenn Aeris. The evidence for this attribution is unusually solid, resting on multiple independent primary sources that corroborate one another: (1) the autograph score held by the Museum of Bretonic Music (BM-MS-742.1), whose title-page inscription 'Nolwenn Aeris – Carn Breac, Feb 17 1978' was confirmed by infra-red photography to have been written in the same ink layer as the musical notation [P2]; (2) a certified deposit at the National Works Registration Agency (Entry 1979-4221), where Aeris affirmed sole authorship, sealed with the Chief Registrar's seal [P1]; and (3) a 1981 Lirien Hall concert programme documenting the world première with 'music by Nolwenn Aeris,' plus a contemporaneous margin note that the composer was present and took a bow [P3]. Secondary sources reinforce this: the choral survey record cites the museum autograph [P5, citing P2], and a 2022 musicology article cites the NWRA registration [P4, citing P1]. Because the three foundational sources (P1, P2, P3) are independent originals — a manuscript, a legal registration, and a performance programme — and the secondary sources simply confirm them, the attribution to Nolwenn Aeris is very well established. The only caveat is that all of these are illustrative/example sources, so the conclusion is only as reliable as those records themselves.

All available sources name silverleaf fungus as the signature ingredient of Narakiri Emberpot. This claim appears very solidly supported, resting on multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) a firsthand ethnographic observation in Anaya Peregrine's 1877 field diary (P3), where the cook herself calls it the signature ingredient; (2) a laboratory GC-MS analysis of carbonised residue from a 9th-century vessel (P2), which identifies a metabolite unique to silverleaf fungus as the dominant peak with >99.2% confidence; and (3) a Year 544 NR Royal Kitchens Ledger entry (P1) explicitly mandating it as the signature ingredient. These three primary sources are independent of one another (each cites nothing external and spans different eras and evidence types — archival, chemical, and observational). The remaining two sources (P4 and P5) are not independent corroboration but secondary summaries: P4 merely restates the ledger entry P1, and P5 merely quotes Peregrine's diary P3. So while the effective count of distinct evidence is three rather than five, the convergence of documentary, archaeological-chemical, and eyewitness evidence makes the identification of silverleaf fungus unusually well established.

The commonly quoted record is 14.7 seconds, set by Arin Kjell on 12 August 2023. This figure is very solidly documented, supported by multiple independent original sources that corroborate one another. The primary evidence includes: (1) a contemporaneous judge's field notebook entry [P3] recording Kjell's 14.7 s finish, verified by primary clock and back-up handheld with legal wind; (2) an Omnia-Tech photogate timing certificate [P2] showing a raw gate interval of 14.700 s with ±0.002 s systematic error, certified to meet officials as 14.7 s; and (3) the Official Register of Results from the Aerothalon Executive Council [P1], which lists 14.7 s as the current standing record (last amended 3 Jan 2024). Secondary reports — cliffring-history.example [P5] (citing the notebook P3) and sportstats.today.example [P4] (citing the timing certificate P2) — trace back to these primary sources rather than adding independent evidence. Because both the instrumented timing chain and the official register independently confirm the same value, the 14.7 s figure is well established and consistently attested.

Myrrell's Crossing is said to have been founded in 1675 — specifically, the royal charter dates its legal establishment to 12 June 1675. The evidence for this date is unusually strong and well established. It rests on three independent primary sources: (1) the Royal Patent Roll charter (P1), which explicitly constitutes the township on 12 June 1675, bearing the governor's original signature and province seal; (2) a contemporaneous St Matthew's Parish baptism register entry from 1676 noting the settlement was 'founded 1675' (P3); and (3) Surveyor Elias Thrumm's 1681 field book, which references boundary stones 'previously planted' when the town 'was first staked out in 1675' (P2). These three original sources agree and corroborate one another, and each is a near-contemporaneous document rather than a later reconstruction. The secondary sources — the County Heritage Board fact sheet (P5, citing P3) and the town history book (P4, citing P1) — merely restate and rely on these primary records, so they add confidence but not independent evidence. Overall, the 1675 founding date is very solidly documented.

The commonly reported melting point of Jensuric nitridate is 2420 °C. This figure is fairly well established, because it rests on three mutually independent primary measurements rather than a single source repeatedly citing itself. Specifically: (1) Wernstrom's 1983 induction-furnace/optical-pyrometer test (P1, ±5 °C), (2) a 2016 DSC/STA measurement giving a melting peak at 2420 °C (P3), and (3) the National Materials Registry's certified sealed-crucible fusion assay from 1995 (P2, ±8 °C). These agree closely on 2420 °C despite using different methods, dates, and operators, which strengthens confidence. The remaining sources are secondary and add no independent evidence: the Industrial Chemistry Manual (P4) simply cites the registry (P2), and the Materials Property Digest (P5) simply cites the DSC file (P3). So while the number itself is robustly supported by convergent independent data, one should note the DSC onset was slightly lower (2412 °C) and reported uncertainties are on the order of ±5–8 °C.

Isidro Talmarin was born in Lanthirne (specifically recorded as being born there on 3 April 1784). The evidence for this is very solid and well-established, resting on multiple independent primary sources that converge on the same birthplace: (1) the Saint Torval parish baptismal register of 12 April 1784 [P1], an original ink-on-vellum entry stating he was 'nacido en la ciudad de Lanthirne'; (2) the first-hand maternal diary of his mother, Beatriz Novoa de Talmarin, dated 3 March 1784 [P3], giving a contemporaneous personal account of his birth in Lanthirne; and (3) the 1810 Provincial Enumeration census [P2], a civil/non-ecclesiastical record listing his place of birth as Lanthirne separately from his residence. Secondary sources corroborate these: the biographical dictionary [P4] cites the baptismal register [P1], and a historian's account [P5] cites the census [P2]. Because the claim is supported by several independent original documents (ecclesiastical, personal, and civil) rather than a single source echoed repeatedly, the attribution to Lanthirne is strongly established. One minor caveat: the mother's diary is dated 3 March while the baptism entry gives the birth date as 3 April, a small date discrepancy that does not affect the agreement on the birthplace itself.

Common online references attribute the word “flindel” to the Eldurossa market, where it is said to have originated as a local term for a small metal spring-pin fastening. This attribution is fairly well supported by multiple independent primary sources that agree on the market as the site of use: a 1421 Treasury Ledger recording the word in a customs duty schedule [P1], and a 1503 first-hand travel diary of Lorrein Vask recording vendors calling it out orally [P3]. Two secondary sources build on these — the Lexicon Society Bulletin [P4] relies on the 1421 ledger [P1], and the Annual Etymology Review [P5] relies on the 1503 diary [P3] — so they are not truly independent of the primary records but do corroborate the same origin story. Notably, the earliest evidence is actually earlier than either of those written records: a radiocarbon-dated (AMS) oak stall board inscribed “flindel 4 scats” in Old Eldish runic, dated to roughly 1285 ± 25 CE [P2], which pushes documented use back to the late 13th century and independently corroborates the Eldurossa-market association through physical, not textual, evidence. So the claim that “flindel” originates from (or at least was in early use at) the Eldurossa market is reasonably firmly grounded, resting on converging primary evidence of three different kinds — fiscal record, eyewitness diary, and a scientifically dated artifact. The main caveats: the two secondary references merely echo single primary sources rather than adding independent confirmation, and the sources establish where the word was in early *use*, which is not strictly the same as proving the word was coined there rather than adopted from elsewhere. (All sources here are fictional/example domains, so this should be treated as illustrative rather than a real-world etymology.)

The figure cited is 37.2% of households in Nyrom Kesh relying entirely (sole income source) on shellfruit farming in 2011. This figure is well established and unusually robust: it appears identically across four independent original sources measured through different methods and samples — the Department of Statistics Provincial Household Economic Survey (P1, weighted base 30,612; 11,384 households), the Nyrom Kesh Shellfruit Growers' Cooperative enumerator ledger (P3, 8,609/23,139), and the University of Kyrom Faculty of Agronomy Livelihood Baseline Study (P2, 427/1,148). The two secondary sources both trace back to these primaries: Agrireview Weekly (P4) cites the Department of Statistics report (P1), and the Kaldé Institute policy brief (P5) cites the cooperative ledgers (P3). Because three methodologically distinct primary sources independently converge on exactly 37.2% — and the secondary sources add no independent confirmation but simply relay the primaries — the figure is firmly established. (One minor caveat: the exact identity of the percentage across such different sample sizes is striking and could warrant checking that the sources are truly independent rather than reproducing one another's rounded figure.)

The person credited with the first complete ropeboard traversal of the Torqual under-river tunnels is Kephra Odun, who is recorded as completing the continuous 11.8-km subterranean traverse (North Sink to South Sink) on 4 June 1993. This attribution is very solidly documented. It rests on multiple independent, mutually corroborating original sources: (1) a first-hand expedition logbook entry by surveyor Marta Leng, made the same day and archived shortly after (Accession TRQ-LB1993); (2) an independent instrument dataset from Geodata-Labs (TTRO-06-1993) recording start/end timestamps and a calculated 11.83-km path, checksum-verified within days; and (3) an official first-completion certificate from the Speleological Registry of Novare (Record ID TR-1594), based on in-person inspection by two registry inspectors. The two secondary sources (CaveAdventures and Unified Speleopedia) simply trace back to these primary records — the review to the logbook (P1) and the encyclopedia to the registry certificate (P2) — so they add no independent evidence but do show consistent downstream consensus. Notably, the strongest support comes from three independent primary sources that agree on the person, date, route, and distance, which makes the attribution well established.

The saying "Silence sharpens the arrow" is commonly credited to Efran Qorlen. The evidence for this attribution is unusually solid and mutually reinforcing. The primary source is Qorlen's own field diary (folio 47, dated 3 May 1842) [P1], where he recorded the line in the margin; a 2021 archivist's note reports that infrared imaging confirmed the ink matches other authenticated pages in his hand, with no later editorial marks. This is the earliest verifiable appearance, and the Proverb Companion [P4] relies on it, citing handwriting and ink-dating analyses. Later corroboration comes from official state endorsement: the Royal Gazette of Talvennia (1888) [P3] formally attributed the proverb to Qorlen for state-printed school primers, and the Quote History Journal [P5] (drawing on P3) notes this consolidated his authorship across curricula and anthologies. A marble plaque installed in 1911 at the Arrowmakers' Guild Hall [P2] also inscribes the line under his name, with weathering analysis supporting the original installation date.

Caveats worth noting: all sources trace back to a small set of originals. The strongest evidence (the autograph diary) is the earliest, but the physical/forensic claims (ink-dating, IR imaging, weathering analysis) come from archivist and editorial notes rather than independently published technical reports, so a reader cannot fully verify the analyses themselves. The 1888 Gazette and 1911 plaque post-date the diary by decades and largely reflect an official designation rather than independent evidence of authorship. Also note this appears to be a fictional/example corpus (all domains are '.example'). Within that corpus, however, the attribution to Efran Qorlen is well-established and consistent across an autograph source and multiple independent later confirmations.

Lake Quirellen is reported to have a maximum depth of 842 m, making it the deepest lake on the Thornvale Plateau. This figure is very well established. It is supported by three fully independent primary sources using different methods and spanning nearly five decades: a 1974 mechanical sounding-weight survey by Brown & Sons Dredging Co. (three repeat trials, ±1 m), the National Geological Institute's 2019 multi-beam sonar survey (NGI-TB-19-117, ±2 m), and the Orbital Hydroscience Laboratory's 2021 green-wavelength LiDAR bathymetry (DR-OHL-2021-07, stdev 3.6 m). The remaining sources (World Lakes Almanac 2022 and Explorer's Travel Atlas 2023) are secondary references that simply cite the NGI and OHL surveys respectively, so they add no independent evidence. The agreement of three independent methods to the same 842 m value, all within small stated uncertainties, makes this a robustly corroborated figure.

The reputed lifespan of the Sundrelle glimmerhare is about 27 years in the wild. However, this figure is less well founded than the number of citations suggests, because the sources trace back to independent original records that happen to coincide on '27 years,' and the derivative sources don't cross-check each other. There are two genuinely independent modern primary sources: (1) the Northern Sundrelle Prefectural Wildlife Registry [P1], based on capture-recapture of tag R-331 tracked 14 May 2001 to 2 June 2028 — which actually spans about 27 years; and (2) the Institute for Remote Fauna Telemetry collar GLM-12-A07 [P2], with continuous signal from DOY 102/1994 to DOY 101/2021 (27 years). The Life-History Synopsis [P5] simply restates the telemetry study [P2], and the Practical Handbook [P4] restates the registry [P1], so these two do not add independent confirmation. A third source, the 1879–1896 field notebook of Dr. Lestange [P3], also reports a doe reaching 27 years, but this rests on an assumption about adult dentition at first capture and is anecdotal and old, so it is weaker evidence. Additionally, some of the primary figures have caveats: the telemetry record ends only because the battery expired, so it establishes a minimum living interval rather than a true maximum lifespan, and the registry age depends on age-at-banding assumptions. So while multiple sources agree on roughly 27 years, the figure is best described as a reputed/verified-minimum maximum age supported by a couple of independent capture-recapture and telemetry records rather than a rigorously established true maximum lifespan.

The available websites all give 1798 as the invention year for the Crenlow siphon-stitcher. This date appears very well-established within these sources, as it is supported by multiple independent-seeming primary documents: Ephraim Crenlow's own workshop journal dated 3 April 1798 recording the first working prototype (P2), a British Patent Office register showing a patent granted 14 February 1798 (P1), and a Port of Liverpool customs ledger from 1798 logging the device and marking its year of invention as 1798 (P3). The secondary sources (P4 and P5) simply cite these primary records. So relative to the retrieved material, the 1798 date is strongly and consistently corroborated. Two important caveats: (1) all corroboration comes from a small closed set of interlinked '.example' domains, which are illustrative/placeholder sources rather than verifiable real-world archives, so this consistency does not amount to genuine external verification; and (2) the primary documents actually point to slightly different milestones within 1798 (patent grant in February, prototype completion in April, importation in September), which is internally coherent for a single year but shows that '1798' bundles together distinct events rather than a single pinpointed invention date.
